title: WKT / GeoJSON Helper: Two Text Geographies
description: Work between WKT and GeoJSON with the WKT / GeoJSON Helper — inspect either format on the map and understand how they correspond. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the WKT POINT (-73.9855 40.758) and the GeoJSON {"type": "Point", "coordinates": [-73.9855, 40.758]} are the same Times Square in two dialects — this helper is where the translation gets inspected.
quick_answer: The WKT / GeoJSON Helper works between the two text formats of modern geography — Well-Known Text and GeoJSON — letting you paste spatial data, inspect it on the map and see how the formats correspond. Both are read locally in your browser; nothing is uploaded.
steps_intro: Two dialects, one geography — learn the correspondence by looking:

use_cases.title: Moving between PostGIS and the web

body.t: Databases speak WKT (ST_AsText), APIs speak GeoJSON. The helper is the phrasebook on the border — validate the WKT side with the
when the database's output smells wrong.
A ring that renders inside-out or a point in the sea: paste both versions and compare geometry against the map until the guilty transformation confesses.
Students meet WKT's parentheses and GeoJSON's nested arrays side by side — the correspondence (rings, members, collections) clicks in one sitting.
Docs need the same geometry in both formats; generate one, translate, verify on the map — three steps, no hand-typed coordinates.

GeoJSON (RFC 7946) recommends the right-hand rule — exterior rings counterclockwise in lon/lat space; WKT (as most databases write it) does not enforce orientation. A polygon can be valid in both yet wound oppositely — the map looks identical, the spec compliance differs, and this is the difference nobody warns you about.
WKT has POINT EMPTY; GeoJSON has "coordinates": [] or a null geometry. Translating emptiness is a decision, not a default — the helper surfaces empty members instead of silently dropping them.

popular_table.title: Format correspondence
popular_table.note: Both formats are longitude-first. The agreement ends most arguments; the differences (properties, empties, orientation customs) live in the table above.

faq: It lets you inspect and work between the formats on the map — paste one form and see the geometry, with the corresponding form presented for copying. The map is the referee: if both forms draw the same shape, the correspondence is right.
Numbers carry as written; decimal trimming is a deliberate act (and a data-quality decision), never a conversion side-effect here.
GeoJSON Features carry properties; WKT has no property concept. Converting WKT→GeoJSON yields bare geometry (or a Feature with empty properties) — nothing is invented to fill the gap.
Both carry a third ordinate (WKT marks it with Z; GeoJSON just adds the number). The helper preserves the third value through inspection.

GeoJSON (RFC 7946) is WGS84 lon/lat by definition — no CRS member. WKT may travel with an SRID in EWKT form. Mixing a projected WKT into a GeoJSON viewer is the classic silent error; the map exposes it instantly (your city lands at metres-scale coordinates near 0,0).
Unparseable text is reported as such — the WKT Validator diagnoses WKT syntax specifically; GeoJSON has its own validator in this family.
Store where it will be queried: spatial databases index WKT/WKB natively; web pipelines flow GeoJSON. The helper's existence is the argument for not marrying one.
